newsitem.title: USA: Albright, starting Asia tour, heads for Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: Albright, starting Asia tour, heads for Vietnam.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright left here on Wednesday for Hanoi on a visit to strengthen ties with Vietnam, a country with deep historical significance for the United States.
"She's going to work on the relationship, try to advance our relations with one of the more important countries in southeast Asia," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

The Vietnam visit is the first leg of an Asian tour by Albright, who was scheduled to go on to Cambodia, although officials have indicated this looks less likely than before because of security concerns.
If she does not go to Cambodia on this trip, she probably will go there in late July when she attends an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meeting in Malaysia.
Albright's last stop on this tour is Hong Kong, where she will attend the July 1 transfer of the British colony to Chinese control.

In Vietnam, Albright goes from Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City, formerly Saigon, where she is expected to break ground for a U.S. consulate which officials expect to become one of the biggest U.S. visa-issuing posts in the region.

Albright, the first secretary of state to visit Vietnam since a breakthrough 1995 trip by Warren Christopher, will explore progres in accounting for U.S. servicemen missing from the Vietnam War, a key issue in bilateral ties, Burns said.

U.S. and Vietnamese authorities are trying to account for more than 2,100 U.S. servicemen listed as missing in action (MIA) in Indochina, more than 1,500 of them in Vietnam, from the war that ended in 1975.
In the war, the United States backed South Vietnam, which was defeated by North Vietnamese and southern communist guerrilla forces.
Burns said Albright would also discuss economic relations, human rights and broader political issues when she meets key Vietnamese government officials.
Since the United States lifted a trade embargo in 1994, more than 400 American firms have set up operations in Vietnam and hundreds pursue business there from U.S. and regional headquarters.

"The U.S.-Vietnam economic relationship is one of the handful in the world which should experience dramatic growth in the years to come and create jobs for Americans as exports grow," Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Jeff Bader told Congress recently.
But for this to happen, "Vietnam needs to eliminate trade barriers and continue to develop an institutional and legal framework for meeting the needs of American business," he said.
